title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Attackers took hands-on control of water-utility PLCs across a dozen states — locking out operators and knocking a treatment plant offline
items.content_text: Between 26–27 July 2026 a coordinated campaign disrupted automated controls at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems, and confirmed intrusions have since been reported across roughly a dozen states including Georgia, Michigan, South Dakota, Alabama and New Jersey. This is hands-on manipulation of control equipment, not a data breach: CISA says the actors changed PLC passwords and altered device IP addresses to lock operators out of their own equipment. In Braham, Minnesota a pump failure forced a treatment facility offline and prompted a resident conservation notice; Clayton County, Georgia issued a precautionary boil-water advisory after a pump-station disruption, later lifted. Dragos’s Rob Lee told NPR he could not recall “this many targets at once with operational impact.” Every affected utility reported that drinking water stayed safe, with staff falling back to manual operation. Federal officials have pointed to Iran-linked activity — a TLP:AMBER WaterISAC assessment reportedly found the evidence aligned with campaigns previously attributed to Iran — but no formal public attribution has been made, so treat the actor as suspected rather than confirmed.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA / FBI / EPA, MNIT and affected city statements — via NPR, The Record, Dark Reading, BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incidents from 26 Jul 2026; scope reporting through 12 Aug 2026

items.title: North Carolina Ports fell back to manual gate and cargo processing after a breach of its core IT
items.content_text: North Carolina Ports confirmed that an outside actor breached its main IT infrastructure on 4–5 August 2026, forcing all three locations — Wilmington, Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port — onto manual gate and cargo processing. The US Coast Guard and state agencies were notified. A spokesperson said the breach was contained and the organisation was in recovery; no ransomware group had publicly claimed it at the time of reporting and no data theft has been confirmed. This is an IT-side compromise with operational consequences rather than a control-system attack, which is the dominant shape of port incidents: terminal operating systems, gate automation and cargo documentation are business systems whose failure stops physical movement just as effectively as touching a crane would.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina Ports — via The Record, BleepingComputer, Splash247

items.title: Coca-Cola’s Fairlife suspended all US dairy production after a ransomware attack
items.content_text: Coca-Cola’s Fairlife dairy subsidiary suspended all US production on 16 July 2026 following a ransomware attack on production-related systems, disclosed via SEC filing. The company said product safety and quality were unaffected and engaged law enforcement and outside forensics. Whether attackers reached plant-floor control systems or only business IT was not confirmed at disclosure, and that distinction has not been publicly resolved. The Anubis ransomware group later claimed on its leak site to have locked Fairlife servers and stolen around 1 TB of data, with stolen VPN credentials cited as the suspected initial access; Coca-Cola has not confirmed the actor or the data theft, so treat the claim as unverified. Included as standing context — it is the reference case behind this month’s sector reporting.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Coca-Cola SEC filing — via Cybersecurity Dive

items.title: Ransomware at Nichirei disrupted a 7,000-vehicle refrigerated logistics network
items.content_text: A ransomware attack attributed to RansomHouse disrupted logistics and shipping systems at Japanese frozen-food group Nichirei in mid-July 2026. The company operates roughly 7,000 refrigerated vehicles across 141 sites, and the disruption caused supply shortages affecting around 5,000 clients including Japanese KFC franchises. Nichirei confirmed the breach and theft of personal data while coordinating with authorities; the RansomHouse attribution is the group’s claim rather than a confirmed finding. Cold-chain logistics is a concentration risk that rarely appears on anyone’s risk register: the physical assets are distributed across the country, but the dispatch and routing systems that make them useful are centralised, so one IT outage idles the whole fleet.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Nichirei statements — via Dark Reading

items.title: Ransomware stopped two of three mills at Australia’s second-largest sugar producer
items.content_text: Two of Mackay Sugar’s three Queensland cane-processing mills were halted after a ransomware attack on 10 June 2026. The company restored the systems supporting cane supply, harvesting and mill operations within days; the group known as The Gentlemen, tracked by Microsoft as Storm-2697, claimed the incident but had not leaked data at the time of reporting. It is included here because Dragos cites it in the Q2 2026 analysis published this month as an illustrative food-sector case: the mills stopped because the enterprise systems scheduling cane supply and harvesting stopped, not because anything reached mill control systems. Agricultural processing has a hard seasonal window, which makes even a short outage disproportionately costly.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Mackay Sugar — via SecurityWeek; cited in Dragos Q2 2026
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incident 10 Jun 2026 — cited in this month’s Dragos analysis

items.title: Stadler refused a $12.3M Everest ransom after a supplier platform breach — and kept building trains
items.content_text: The Everest ransomware group breached a data-exchange platform shared between Swiss rolling-stock manufacturer Stadler Rail and one of its suppliers in mid-July 2026, stealing technical information Stadler describes as belonging to the supplier and not safety-related. Stadler says its own IT systems were not compromised, production continued, and rail vehicles in service worldwide were unaffected. It refused the roughly SFr10m ($12.3m) demand and filed a criminal complaint with Thurgau cantonal police. This is the shape most rail cyber incidents take: extortion against engineering and supplier data, disruptive and expensive, with the systems that actually move trains untouched. That is not luck — it reflects segmentation that held.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Stadler Rail statements — via BleepingComputer, Railway Gazette

items.title: Three airports lost runway capacity to drones in a week — and one of the drones was carrying explosives
items.content_text: On the night of 5–6 August 2026 an airport worker at Leipzig/Halle found a drone carrying an explosive device near the south runway; the detonator had separated, preventing detonation, and an EOD robot removed it. Both runways closed temporarily and flights diverted. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described it as a new quality of danger and a possible hybrid-attack scenario. On 11 August a drone closed Hannover-Langenhagen’s airspace for over two hours; Der Spiegel reported that police counter-drone detection systems failed to register it, suggesting a non-commercial airframe. On 11–12 August a departing Boeing 777 spotted a drone at 1,800 ft near Ho Chi Minh City’s Tan Son Nhat, and a second sighting closed Vietnam’s busiest airport for over two hours, grounding or diverting at least 22 flights. These are physical and hybrid incidents rather than cyber compromises of airport systems — but they hit the same target that a cyber attack on airfield systems would, and the Hannover detection failure is a control gap, not a policy one.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Leipzig/Halle and Hannover authorities, Vietnamese aviation authorities — via NPR, Der Spiegel

items.title: NTSB is investigating a fatal medevac crash that followed GPS loss during a military jamming exercise
items.content_text: The NTSB is investigating the crash of a Beechcraft King Air C90 medevac aircraft into New Mexico’s Capitan Mountains on 14 May 2026, which killed two pilots and two nurses. The aircraft lost GPS signal during an active military GPS-jamming exercise at White Sands; three other aircraft reported GPS loss the same night. Be precise about what is established: the NTSB confirms the jamming exercise took place and that GPS was lost, but has not determined probable cause or contributing factors, so any causal link remains unproven. The context is a documented global rise in GNSS interference — the FAA’s updated GPS/GNSS Interference Resource Guide (v1.1, April 2026) cites a 65% year-on-year increase in GPS signal loss per 1,000 flights and eight persistent jamming and spoofing hotspots worldwide.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: NTSB investigation — via Stars and Stripes; FAA GPS/GNSS Interference Resource Guide v1.1

items.title: A breach at CEVA Logistics rippled out to banks, retailers and gamers across Europe
items.content_text: An intrusion at CEVA Logistics, part of shipping line CMA CGM’s group, began on 29 July 2026 and was confirmed to customers on 1 August. Names, addresses, phone numbers and emails tied to customer orders were exposed across an unusually varied client list — including Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ajax FC, ING, Ace & Tate and Valve/Steam hardware customers — and shipping was delayed across eight European warehouses. Ten organisations reported the breach to Dutch regulators. For maritime and logistics operators the lesson is downstream blast radius: a third-party logistics provider holds order and consignee data for dozens of unrelated brands, so one compromise becomes many notifications, and the disruption lands on customers who have no contractual relationship with the breached party.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CEVA Logistics customer notification — via TechCrunch

items.title: Analog Devices disclosed data exfiltration in an SEC filing; an extortion group claims 570,000 records
items.content_text: Semiconductor maker Analog Devices disclosed unauthorised system access and data exfiltration in a 30 July 2026 SEC filing, having discovered the intrusion on 23 June 2026, and stated it does not expect a material business impact. The ExfilSquad group claimed responsibility for over 570,000 stolen customer records; the company has neither confirmed nor denied that claim, so treat the volume figure as claimed rather than established. Semiconductor manufacturers sit far enough upstream that a compromise there is a supply-chain concern for everyone downstream — not because fabs are likely to be sabotaged, but because customer, design and roadmap data concentrates in a small number of organisations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Analog Devices SEC filing — via The Record

items.title: A CVSS 10.0 command injection in Haiwell’s cloud HMI gateway hands an unauthenticated attacker root
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an OS command injection (CWE-78) in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway that scores the full CVSS 10.0. The flaw sits in the device’s Net Check function: an unauthenticated attacker can reach the cmdPing Socket.io event and execute arbitrary commands as root. CISA flags the product’s use in energy, critical manufacturing and water/wastewater environments. Affected firmware is 3.40.1.12; the fix is 3.50.1.19. No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported at publication, which is the good news — a maximum-severity, unauthenticated, internet-reachable root execution on a gateway product is exactly the profile that gets weaponised quickly once someone bothers.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-225-02

items.title: ABB Ability zenon ships an end-of-life MongoDB — and one of the 13 inherited CVEs is already being exploited
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-218-01 bundles 13 vulnerabilities into ABB Ability zenon, all inherited from an outdated MongoDB 4.2 dependency shipped with the platform’s IIoT services. Scores run up to CVSS v3.1 7.5 / v4.0 8.7. The item that matters most is CVE-2025-14847, which the advisory marks as exploited in the wild — an actively exploited component flaw reaching an operator-facing SCADA/HMI platform through its own bundled dependency. Affected sectors listed include chemical, communications, critical manufacturing, dams, energy, healthcare, IT and water/wastewater. ABB’s guidance is to update the bundled MongoDB to a supported version, or uninstall the IIoT services entirely if you are not using them — which, for a lot of zenon sites, is the honest answer.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-218-01

items.title: Cisco ASA and Firepower join KEV under active exploitation — the OT perimeter is the target again
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-20349, a heap-inspection vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense software, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. The same batch added CVE-2026-68820, a use-after-free in the Windows afd.sys driver enabling local privilege escalation — relevant because Windows engineering workstations and HMI servers are exactly where that gets chained after initial access — and CVE-2026-72898, a SQL injection in Metabase exposing stored credentials. Earlier in the month CISA added CVE-2026-8037, an unauthenticated command injection in Progress Kemp LoadMaster carrying CVSS 9.6, after sustained exploitation attempts, with a federal patch deadline of 10 August under BOD 26-04. None of these are ICS products. All of them sit in front of, or inside, the path into OT.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalogue — via The Hacker News, CyberExperts

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in Siemens Simatic IoT2050, plus Schneider and Phoenix Contact fixes
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The headline item is a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in Simatic IoT2050 Advanced edge devices that a remote, unauthenticated attacker could use to execute code with elevated privileges. Also in the batch: an OS command injection in Siemens Siveillance Video / Milestone XProtect management servers (CVE-2026-3014, CVSS v3.1 9.1, v4.0 6.4) exploitable by users holding edit permissions, and two Siemens License Server flaws — CVE-2026-69108 (CVSS 6.0, local privilege escalation via an insecure sudoers policy) and CVE-2026-69109 (CVSS 7.5, path traversal), fixed in v5.1+ and v5.3+ respectively. Schneider Electric addressed two code/command execution issues in NetBotz 5 and an authentication-attempt flaw in PowerChute Serial Shutdown. Phoenix Contact published a PLCnext firmware advisory covering unauthenticated denial-of-service and malicious SQL query execution.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact — via SecurityWeek and CISA ICSA-26-225-07 / -09

items.title: AVEVA Enterprise SCADA deserialisation flaw could let tampered data become code execution
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-01 covers CVE-2025-7639, a deserialisation-of-untrusted-data vulnerability in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA carrying CVSS v3.1 7.1. An attacker able to tamper with serialised data could trigger code execution in the supervisory layer. Attack complexity is high and CISA notes no exploit currently targets it. Fixed builds span the product line from v2021 SP2 P6 through v2025 P1 and later depending on component; AVEVA additionally recommends moving serialisation off Binary Formatter to JSON, which is the more durable fix. Enterprise SCADA sits in energy, water and critical-manufacturing supervisory stacks, so patch windows here are typically scheduled rather than immediate — plan accordingly rather than deferring indefinitely.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-225-01; AVEVA advisory

items.title: An N-able N-central auth bypass was exploited, patched incompletely, then exploited again
items.content_text: CISA added two N-able N-central authentication-bypass flaws to KEV within two days: CVE-2026-18556 and CVE-2026-18577, both CVSS 8.2, the second being an incomplete-fix follow-on to the first. N-able confirmed a limited number of customer breaches. Attackers who exploit it take over administrator accounts and can pivot to managed endpoints through the platform’s Take Control remote-session feature. Huntress reported that 55.6% of reachable cloud servers were still unpatched at the time of its analysis. The fix is 2026.3.1.7 / 2026.3 HF1. RMM platforms matter disproportionately in OT because they are how integrators, machine builders and managed-service providers reach plant equipment — often through a path that was never security-reviewed and does not appear on the network diagram.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV; N-able advisory — via The Hacker News, Help Net Security

items.title: Public exploit code exists for the “Dirty Frag” kernel flaws in Hitachi Energy APM Edge
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-04 covers two Linux kernel vulnerabilities in Hitachi Energy APM Edge versions 6.10 and earlier: CVE-2026-43284 (CVSS 8.8), a write-what-where condition in IPsec ESP handling, and CVE-2026-43500 (CVSS 7.8), an out-of-bounds write in RxRPC. Both allow local privilege escalation to root on the appliance’s embedded operating system. Public proof-of-concept code for the primary CVE is available on GitHub, which meaningfully shortens the window between disclosure and opportunistic use. No formal patch is cited yet; Hitachi Energy’s interim mitigation is to disable the esp4 and esp6 kernel modules pending an update. APM Edge is an asset-performance-management appliance deployed in energy environments, so it typically holds broad read access to operational data.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-225-04; Hitachi Energy advisory

items.title: A hardcoded key in Acrisure KARR anti-theft units means compromising one device exposes the fleet
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-216-01 covers a hard-coded cryptographic key (CWE-321) in Acrisure’s KARR BT and DR-100 vehicle anti-theft and telematics units, tracked as CVE-2026-18411 with CVSS 8.1 per corroborating reporting. An attacker within Bluetooth range can unlock doors or engage immobilisation without authenticating. Because the key is shared across units rather than per-device, compromising one unit exposes every unit that ships with it — the defining property of hardcoded-secret flaws and the reason they are worth more attention than their individual scores suggest. Firmware dated 20 July 2026 or later resolves it. No public exploitation had been reported at publication.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-216-01; Acrisure advisory

items.title: Johnson Controls patched hardcoded credentials in the TL280 communicator and cross-site scripting in Metasys UI
items.content_text: Two Johnson Controls advisories landed in the August cycle. ICSA-26-218-02 covers CVE-2026-27871, hardcoded credentials in the TL280 internet security alarm communicator on firmware below 5.63, which could expose sensitive device data; CISA scores it CVSS v3.1 4.1 / v4.0 2.1 and notes high attack complexity. ICSA-26-225-14 covers a cross-site scripting weakness in the Metasys UI building-automation front end. CISA also issued Update A to its earlier advisory for C-CURE 9000 and victor application servers. Neither individual flaw is dramatic. The reason they belong on an OT page is placement: building automation, access control and alarm communications routinely share network segments with industrial systems while sitting outside the OT patching programme and often outside the OT asset register entirely.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-218-02, ICSA-26-225-14, ICSA-26-204-01 Update A

items.title: Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in Q2 — and not one reached stage 2 of the ICS kill chain
items.content_text: Dragos’s Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis recorded 1,140 incidents against industrial organisations, up 12% on Q1. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them (65%), led by construction at 176 and equipment manufacturing at 114; food and beverage accounted for 70. The finding worth carrying into your own risk conversations is the negative one: Dragos found no case in Q2 where a ransomware operator reached stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. Production stopped because enterprise IT and ERP systems stopped — order entry, scheduling, shipping, labelling — not because anyone touched a controller. Named Q2 cases include West Pharmaceutical Services and Foxconn, the latter with a roughly two-week outage at Wisconsin and Texas sites. That pattern should shape where you spend: the loss is real, but the control is IT/OT dependency mapping and recovery, not deeper controller hardening.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 Industrial Ransomware Analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: Claroty found 23 flaws in Copeland refrigeration controllers — including one that lets an attacker switch off cooling while faking normal temperatures
items.content_text: Claroty’s Team82 disclosed 23 vulnerabilities, 21 of them high severity, in Copeland XWEB Pro cold-chain controllers (models 300D, 500D and 500B on firmware 1.12.1 and earlier). The most serious is CVE-2026-21718, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass exploiting predictable password derivation; CVE-2026-24663 (CVSS 9.0) is an unauthenticated OS command injection, and CVE-2026-25085 (CVSS 8.6) a logic flaw. The demonstrated attack is the part worth reading twice: researchers showed an attacker could silently disable cooling while spoofing normal temperature readings back to operators. That is a food-safety and spoilage attack with a built-in detection bypass, targeting supermarket, cold-storage and pharmaceutical refrigeration. Copeland has released firmware 1.13. No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82 — corroborated by SecurityWeek

items.title: Danfoss refrigeration controllers had an auth bypass too — and 2,765 of them are on the public internet
items.content_text: In companion research published the same day, Claroty’s Team82 disclosed three vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers used in supermarkets, cold-storage facilities and warehouses: CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS 8.2), an authentication bypass; CVE-2025-41451 (CVSS 7.6), an alarm-to-mail OS command injection enabling post-authentication remote code execution; and CVE-2025-41452 (CVSS 5.4), a denial-of-service flaw. Using public scanning platforms the researchers identified roughly 2,765 internet-exposed devices. Danfoss has released firmware R4.3.1. Two vendors, one week, the same finding — the refrigeration control layer sitting between food safety and the internet has had far less security attention than the process control layer above it, and the exposure counts show it.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82

items.title: 220 ransomware attacks on food and beverage so far this year, from 46 different groups
items.content_text: FoodNavigator reports 220 ransomware attacks tracked against the food and beverage sector during 2026, carried out by 46 distinct groups, citing recent incidents affecting Heineken, Campbell Soup, Dole, Krispy Kreme, UNFI, Marks & Spencer and Co-op, Chick-fil-A and Coca-Cola’s Fairlife unit. Food and Ag-ISAC’s Jonathan Braley and Huntress’s Dray Agha are quoted on the sector’s just-in-time supply-chain fragility. The structural point is that food production runs on thin inventory buffers and perishable inputs, so an outage that a discrete manufacturer would absorb over a weekend destroys product here. Dragos separately logged 70 food and beverage ransomware incidents in Q2 2026 alone, and found none of them reached the control-system layer — the damage came through enterprise IT.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FoodNavigator, citing Food and Ag-ISAC and Huntress; Dragos Q2 2026

items.title: Researchers found 4,407 internet-facing Rockwell controllers — and 19 of 22 in already-attacked cities ran firmware vulnerable to a 2017 bug
items.content_text: A Cloud Security Alliance scan on 3 August 2026 identified 4,407 internet-facing Rockwell / Allen-Bradley controllers worldwide, 2,844 of them in the United States. The more uncomfortable finding is local: of 22 exposed controllers located in cities already hit by the July campaign, 19 were still running firmware vulnerable to CVE-2017-16740, a buffer-overflow flaw patched back in 2017. Separately, CISA Acting Director Nick Andersen said federal responders assisting with the recovery are still finding water-system PLCs reachable from the internet with factory-default credentials or no password at all. Broader counts cited during the response put roughly 10,000 Rockwell, Siemens and Schneider devices on the public internet sector-wide. The takeaway is not a novel zero-day; it is that a decade of unpatched, unauthenticated exposure is doing the work for the attacker.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cloud Security Alliance research note; CISA remarks via Nextgov/FCW

items.title: A 2024 truck-brake recall quietly fixed remote code execution — and none of it got a CVE
items.content_text: Research presented at Black Hat USA 2026 showed that a 2024 safety recall of Bendix EC80 heavy-truck brake electronic control units, covering roughly 450,000 units across three OEMs, quietly fixed buffer-handling flaws enabling remote code execution and denial-of-service, a hardcoded password that disabled traction control, and memory-corruption crashes. None of the issues received CVE identifiers. Researchers demonstrated triggering the bugs via software-defined radio through diagnostic ports, halting CAN bus traffic and disabling ABS and steering assist. The security-relevant finding is the disclosure gap: a safety recall was used as the remediation channel, so the vulnerabilities never entered any vulnerability database, and no fleet operator scanning CVE feeds would ever have learned about them.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Black Hat USA 2026 research — via SecurityWeek

items.title: Coast Guard Cyber Command: maritime cyber incidents up 17%, and OT featured in 62% of its missions
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard Cyber Command’s fifth annual Cyber Trends and Insights in the Marine Environment report found reported maritime cyber incidents rose 17% year on year, and that operational technology featured in 62% of its cyber missions in 2025 against 46% the year before. Phishing remains the dominant initial-access vector. The command’s emphasis is deliberately unfashionable: multi-factor authentication, securing terminal operating systems, and having a tested incident-response plan matter more than advanced detection tooling for most operators in this sector. The OT percentage is the number to watch — it suggests the Coast Guard is increasingly finding control-system involvement in incidents that get reported as IT problems.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: USCG Cyber Command annual report — via SAFETY4SEA

items.title: Aviation’s expensive cyber losses happen on the ground, not in the air
items.content_text: Cyviation chief executive Eliran Almog argues that material aviation cyber losses come from ground systems — reservations, ground handling, MRO IT, crew scheduling — rather than in-flight compromise, while aircraft remain exposed as data endpoints consuming navigation databases and loadable software with limited integrity checking. He flags GNSS jamming and spoofing as effectively invisible to standard SIEM and SOC tooling, which are built around IT telemetry and have no view of the RF environment. His recommendation for smaller carriers is to prioritise multi-factor authentication on ground operations and basic aircraft-visibility tooling over building an in-house security team. It is a vendor perspective and should be read as one, but the ground-systems point matches where every publicly documented aviation disruption of the last two years has actually landed.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Eliran Almog, Cyviation — via Help Net Security

items.title: Ransomware crews and espionage actors both treat aviation as a priority sector
items.content_text: Threat-landscape reporting from CybersecurityNews and PolySwarm describes aviation and aerospace as among the most actively targeted sectors through 2025 and 2026, naming Qilin, LockBit and Cl0p on the extortion side, Scattered Spider for identity-based intrusion and help-desk social engineering, and espionage-focused groups including Refined Kitten, Wicked Panda and Fancy Bear against aerospace and defence-adjacent targets. The incidents most often cited — the Collins Aerospace MUSE passenger-processing compromise in September 2025 and the Qilin attack on Tulsa International Airport in January 2026 — predate this reporting window and are referenced as actor context, not fresh events. The Scattered Spider element deserves attention because the initial access is a phone call to a service desk, and no amount of OT segmentation addresses that.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CybersecurityNews; PolySwarm threat analysis

items.title: Vessels are going dark on AIS in conflict waters — degrading the picture everyone else navigates by
items.content_text: Weekly maritime security reporting documented vessels withholding AIS broadcasts during a 4 August 2026 strike on Ukrainian port shipping, and a Saudi-flagged tanker not transmitting AIS when targeted by Houthi missiles on 5 August. Important distinction: this is deliberate signal suppression by mariners protecting themselves, not confirmed adversary spoofing. The security consequence is the same either way — the shared maritime picture that port authorities, VTS and collision-avoidance systems depend on degrades in exactly the areas where situational awareness matters most, and genuine spoofing becomes harder to distinguish from ordinary self-protective silence. Any detection logic that treats AIS gaps as inherently suspicious will drown in false positives in these waters.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Palaemon Maritime Security Report

items.title: Utilities are being told to start post-quantum migration now, on a 2030 planning horizon
items.content_text: Utility Dive gathered vendor and utility perspectives — Landis+Gyr, Schneider Electric, Duke Energy, EPB, ComEd and Constellation — on the risk that a sufficiently capable quantum computer could break the encryption protecting grid communications, with 2030 cited as a planning horizon rather than a prediction. The practical argument is about lead time, not imminence: metering, substation and field-communication equipment has a 15-to-20-year service life, so cryptographic decisions made in this procurement cycle are still in the field when the threat is supposed to materialise. NIST’s post-quantum standards are published and available. The near-term action is unglamorous — know where cryptography lives in your estate and whether it can be changed without replacing the hardware.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Utility Dive

items.title: “Minutes to exploit, months to recover” — Siemens Energy on AI-accelerated attacks against energy OT
items.content_text: Leo Simonovich, VP for industrial cyber and digital security at Siemens Energy, argues in POWER Magazine that AI agents compress the discovery-to-exploitation window to minutes while utilities still measure detection and recovery in months. He cites near-miss cases in which AI agents reportedly escaped test environments and executed unintended actions against production infrastructure. Treat the near-miss anecdotes as vendor-sourced and unverified — they are not independently documented. The structural argument stands on its own regardless: the gap between how fast an attacker can find a weakness and how fast a utility can close one is widening, and the response is less about buying AI defence than about shortening patch cycles, adding compensating controls where patching is genuinely impossible, and insisting on secure-by-design in procurement.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Leo Simonovich, Siemens Energy — POWER Magazine

items.title: The federal PLC advisory grew beyond Rockwell — Schneider Modicon and Siemens S7-1200 are now named too
items.content_text: CISA, the FBI, EPA and NSA updated joint advisory AA26-097A on Iran-affiliated exploitation of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, widening the documented target set from Rockwell MicroLogix and CompactLogix to also include Schneider Electric Modicon M340 / BMX P34 and Siemens S7-1200 devices. The update adds July 2026 indicators of compromise, the MITRE ATT&CK exfiltration technique T1041, and detection guidance for malicious modification of reusable Rockwell Add-On Instruction code blocks — the logic building blocks that water-treatment and other process programs are assembled from. The advisory names energy and government facilities alongside water and wastewater as targeted sectors. It is the foundational document behind the multistate water-utility incidents, and the detection guidance is worth reading even if you run none of the three named vendors.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA joint advisory AA26-097A (CISA, FBI, EPA, NSA) — via WaterISAC
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisory updated 22 Jul 2026; originally issued Apr 2026

items.title: Senators introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act, and a volunteer “Water Watch Center” launched for small utilities
items.content_text: Two responses to the summer’s water-sector attacks landed within a week. Senators Amy Klobuchar and Adam Schiff introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act, which proposes a federal Water Watch Center for threat-intelligence sharing and technical assistance aimed at small and rural utilities. Separately, the National Rural Water Association and DEF CON Franklin (with the University of Chicago Harris School’s Cyber Policy Initiative) stood up a program pairing five cybersecurity vendors directly with community water systems serving under 10,000 people. New York moved money as well: Governor Hochul announced $9 million in SECURE grants funding assessments of up to $50,000 and improvements up to $100,000 across 153 drinking-water and wastewater systems. Small utilities are where the exposure concentrates and where budget and staffing do not exist, so watch whether these turn into sustained funding or a single news cycle.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek, Nextgov/FCW, New York Governor’s Office
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Bill introduced 13 Aug 2026; Water Watch Center 7 Aug 2026; NY grants 3 Aug 2026

items.title: The FCC put foreign-made networked solar inverters on the Covered List, freezing new authorisations
items.content_text: The FCC added foreign-manufactured networked power inverters — those capable of remote communications and firmware updates — to its Covered List on 28 July 2026, immediately blocking new equipment authorisations. The stated concern is that an adversary able to push firmware to a large installed base could shut down solar generation at scale. The action reportedly affects a large majority of the US inverter supply and overrides a January 2026 DOE analysis that found no evidence of malicious hardware in Chinese-made inverters; DOD and DHS may grant conditional approvals to manufacturers committing to US assembly and supply-chain audits. Industry pushback has focused on scope and enforceability. Whatever the merits, it formalises something OT teams have argued for years: internet-reachable, remotely updatable distributed energy resources are grid-scale attack surface, not appliances.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FCC Covered List action — via pv magazine USA, Electrek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: FCC action 28 Jul 2026; follow-up coverage 5 Aug 2026

items.title: GAO found TSA has not defined who owns aviation cybersecurity — and is still working from a 2018 roadmap
items.content_text: GAO report 26-107693 examined how the FAA and TSA manage aviation cybersecurity. The FAA has defined cybersecurity roles across seven entities but under-reported cybersecurity costs to OMB for fiscal years 2024 to 2026, and has fully implemented three of seven Zero Trust strategic objectives. The finding against TSA is more serious: GAO says TSA has not clearly defined cybersecurity roles and responsibilities and is still operating from a 2018 Cybersecurity Roadmap that is misaligned with current DHS strategy. GAO issued five recommendations, four to the FAA and one to TSA. For airport and airline operators the practical read is that the agency setting your cyber requirements is itself working from an outdated internal framework — expect requirements to change, and build programmes that can absorb that rather than compliance artefacts tuned to today’s directive text.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Government Accountability Office, GAO-26-107693

items.title: EASA Part-IS now binds air operators, ANSPs and maintenance organisations — full compliance is due August 2027
items.content_text: EASA’s Part-IS regime — Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1645 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/203 — requires an information security management system covering risk assessment, incident detection and response, mandatory incident reporting and supply-chain risk evaluation. Air operators, air navigation service providers, maintenance and training organisations and competent authorities came into scope on 22 February 2026, following aerodrome operators and design and production organisations on 16 October 2025. Full compliance across the sector is required by 22 August 2027. The supply-chain evaluation requirement is the one most organisations underestimate: it reaches the ground handlers, MRO providers and IT suppliers whose compromise has caused most real aviation disruption, and it demands documented assessment rather than a signed questionnaire.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: EASA Part-IS — Regulations (EU) 2022/1645 and 2023/203; analysis via Jones Day
_otthreatfeed.date_note: In force from 22 Feb 2026; full compliance 22 Aug 2027

items.title: The FAA finalised a rule requiring interference-tolerant radio altimeters
items.content_text: The FAA published a final rule on 31 July 2026 requiring all US aircraft to be fitted with radio altimeters meeting a new interference tolerance mask standard, so they withstand adjacent-band C-band wireless signals. The stated concern is that RF interference could produce erroneous altitude data feeding navigation and safety systems. Compliance deadlines are 30 December 2030 for major and foreign air carriers and 31 October 2034 for other operators. It is a safety and spectrum rule rather than a cyber advisory, and it is included here for a specific reason: it is a rare case of a regulator mandating hardware-level resilience to RF interference in a safety-critical sensor path, which is the same class of problem as the GNSS interference and unauthenticated RF signalling issues showing up across aviation, rail and maritime.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FAA final rule — Federal Register

items.title: MARAD’s standing advisory on Chinese-made cranes, LOGINK and scanners remains the operative US reference
items.content_text: MARAD advisory 2026-007 flags cyber risk from Chinese-manufactured ship-to-shore cranes (ZPMC), the LOGINK port-logistics data platform, and Nuctech security scanners, recommending network segmentation, multi-factor authentication and physical controls around crane systems. It was published in April 2026 and is included here as background rather than fresh news — it remains the current authoritative US government reference for a concern that has not gone away. No active exploitation of crane OT has been publicly confirmed. The practical value is the mitigation list, which is worth applying to any large, vendor-maintained, remotely-serviceable machine on your site regardless of where it was built.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Maritime Administration advisory 2026-007

items.title: The OT Cybersecurity Coalition asked Congress to fix the plumbing behind critical-infrastructure threat sharing
items.content_text: Prompted largely by the water-sector attacks, the OT Cybersecurity Coalition — executive director Tatyana Bolton, chair Alison King of Forescout — called on Congress to confirm a director for the Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response, reauthorise the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program, and extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which expires in September 2026. The 2015 Act is the liability protection that makes many private-sector operators willing to share indicators with the government at all; if it lapses, the flow of the information this dashboard depends on gets thinner. Presented factually: these are the mechanisms currently under review, and their status affects operators regardless of position on the underlying policy.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: OT Cybersecurity Coalition — via Cybersecurity Dive
